detailed_description: The .gitignore Generator helps build a .gitignore file from common stack templates and optional custom rules. Select the templates you need, add any project-specific ignore patterns, generate the combined output, then copy or download the result as .gitignore. It is useful when starting a repository or documenting standard ignore rules. Always review the generated file before committing it, because every project has different build artifacts, environment files, caches, and secret-handling rules.
usage_steps: Select one or more language, framework, or operating-system templates.
Add custom ignore patterns for your project if needed.
Click Generate to combine the selected rules.
Review the output for paths you do or do not want ignored.
Copy the result or download it as a .gitignore file.
Commit the final .gitignore only after checking it against your repository.
usage_examples: Create a Node-focused .gitignore with dependency and build output folders.
Add macOS and Windows system files to a shared repository ignore list.
Include custom rules for local environment files.
Download the result and place it at the root of a new Git repository.

faqs.question: Can I add custom .gitignore rules?
faqs.answer: Yes. The page includes a custom rules area that is appended to the generated output.

faqs.question: Can I download the result?
faqs.answer: Yes. The download action saves the generated text as a .gitignore file.

faqs.question: Should I ignore all environment files?
faqs.answer: Usually you should ignore files containing local secrets, but keep safe example files such as .env.example when your team needs them.

faqs.question: Can a .gitignore remove files already tracked by Git?
faqs.answer: No. .gitignore affects untracked files. Already tracked files must be removed from the index separately.

faqs.question: Should I review generated rules before committing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Make sure the rules do not hide important source files, lockfiles, or configuration that your project needs.
